title: Palantir's Q3 Print Tests Whether Software Margins Can Outrun AI Capex
subtitle: While hyperscalers burn billions on concrete and silicon, Alex Karp is running a 63% cash-flow margin.
summary: Tech investors spent the final session of October punishing Big Tech for historic infrastructure spending, setting up Palantir's third-quarter print as a referendum on software cash conversion. With shares trading at more than fifty times forward revenue, the company must prove its American commercial boom can justify a multiple that leaves no room for error.

bodyHtml:
On Friday, the music stopped for the AI spenders. Wall Street stopped applauding multi-billion-dollar data center blueprints and started checking the receipts. When Amazon torched roughly $42.4 billion in free cash flow over twelve months to bankroll nearly $95 billion in property and equipment, investors ran for the exits. Chips tumbled, the Nasdaq took its worst beating since June, and the market asked an overdue question: who is actually getting paid for AI results right now? Palantir is the mirror image of that trade. Think of Big Tech as the utility company laying high-voltage power lines across the desert. Palantir is the factory boss inside the building, wiring the machinery to turn that raw electricity into finished goods. The company sells software that takes an enterprise’s tangled mess of legacy data and turns it into a real-time operational map. In Palantir’s filings, that engine is called the Ontology—a digital twin of an organization that connects data, business logic, and human action into a single cockpit. Governments use Gotham to coordinate battlefield intelligence, corporations use Foundry to untangle supply chains, and both deploy AIP to build and govern generative AI workflows. Customers pay through subscription- or usage-based pricing.

Crucially, Palantir does not buy gigawatts, finance power plants, or rack millions of GPUs. In its June quarter, capital expenditures totaled just $14.6 million. That is three-quarters of one percent of revenue. While the cloud giants dilute their cash flows pouring concrete, Palantir converts revenue into pure liquidity like a mature software monopoly. Last quarter, it generated $1.220 billion in adjusted free cash flow on $1.935 billion in sales. That is an eye-watering 63% free cash flow margin, backed by a 62% adjusted operating margin. That operating leverage is why Palantir matters to the AI sector. It has become the definitive toll collector sitting on top of other people’s capital expenditures. When companies burn cash experimenting with open-source models, Palantir charges them to make those models work inside their enterprise security perimeters. US commercial revenue exploded 149% year over year in the second quarter to $764 million, driving total revenue up 93%. It is software rent collected on top of someone else's balance sheet. Growth has now accelerated for four straight quarters and the Rule of 40 score is 155. Yet the equity trades roughly flat year to date, about 13% below its October peak. That disconnect explains what has to happen for the stock to re-rate from here. The market is not waiting for growth; it has already paid for perfection. At roughly 54 times fiscal 2026 guided sales and more than 110 times this year's consensus earnings, the multiple is fully stretched. For the stock to push higher, investors need proof that this hypergrowth has lasting duration rather than a quick expiration date. The short seller’s case against that multiple is devastatingly simple. You are paying over 70 times trailing sales for a company whose hypergrowth is almost exclusively an American phenomenon. Strip out the United States and international commercial revenue sat at roughly $181 million last quarter. That is growth estimated at 26%, while US commercial grew nearly six times faster. Total customer count grew less than 24% while revenue jumped 93%. Growth is coming from heavy expansion inside existing accounts, not from sweeping up the broader enterprise universe. Across the field, rival Databricks just crossed a $7 billion revenue run-rate growing north of 80%, yet private marks value it at less than half Palantir's forward multiple. Add in more than $700 million in insider stock sales this year, and any slip in execution risks triggering a violent multiple compression. What would prove the bears right is straightforward. Revenue merely matching company guidance instead of clearing the Street's $2.180 billion consensus, or US commercial growth visibly decelerating. What we are watching is whether international commercial shows any pulse of acceleration, alongside the $2.180 billion revenue hurdle. If Palantir clears that bar and the stock still cannot break out, the market is no longer questioning execution. It is deciding that even the best cash-flow machine in enterprise tech has an upper limit on what it can cost.
